# Correct Discourse

In ancient times, the Son of Heaven <note>the Emperor</note> had a thousand officials and the feudal lords had a hundred officials. When a ruler used these thousand officials to ensure his orders were carried out across all the Chinese states, he was called a King. When a ruler used these hundred officials to ensure his orders were carried out within his own borders, even if the state was not entirely stable, it did not reach the point of collapse or ruin <gloss>the original text uses a word read as "fall" or "losing one's legacy"</gloss>; such a person was called a Lord.

Consider the son of a Sage King. After inheriting the world and holding the official records of land and population, he becomes the head of the Great House of the world. However, if he is untalented and lacks integrity <gloss>literally "not hitting the mark," meaning not upright</gloss>, then internally the common people will hate him, and externally the feudal lords will rebel against him. Those nearby within his borders will not be unified, and the distant feudal lords will not obey. His orders will not even be carried out within his own territory. In extreme cases, the feudal lords will seize and diminish his lands or launch military attacks against him. In such a state, even if he has not yet perished, I say he no longer possesses the world.

When a Sage King dies and his successor is weak and incapable of managing affairs <gloss>literally "tired" or "weak," meaning unable to hold things together</gloss>, he cannot bind the world to him. If the world is without a true ruler, and there is a feudal lord whose virtue is bright and whose prestige has accumulated so that all the people within the four seas wish to have him as their ruler and teacher—yet a violent state remains arrogant and willful—then that lord must punish them. He will certainly not harm innocent people. Punishing the ruler of a violent state is like punishing a solitary fellow <gloss>meaning a man who has lost all support and stands alone</gloss>. One who acts like this can be said to know how to employ the world.

Knowing how to employ the world is what is meant by being a King. Tang and Wu <note>Founders of the Shang and Zhou dynasties</note> did not "take" the world. They cultivated their Way, practiced righteousness, shared benefits with the world, and eliminated the common harms of the world, and thus the world turned to them. Jie and Zhou <note>Last rulers of the Xia and Shang dynasties, cited as tyrants</note> did not "lose" the world <gloss>literally "leave" the world</gloss>; rather, they turned against the virtue of Yu and Tang, disrupted the distinctions of ritual and righteousness, acted like birds and beasts, accumulated wickedness, and so their subjects abandoned them.

<margin>1. The word for "followed" should be read as "fallen," meaning to lose one's legacy.</margin>
<margin>2. "Not middle" means not upright or correct.</margin>
<margin>3. "Tired" refers to being weak and unfit for duty; "suspend" means to bind or connect.</margin>
<margin>4. "Violent states" refers to rulers like Jie and Zhou; "singularly extravagant" means acting with total license; "how" here functions like "then."</margin>
<margin>5. "Solitary fellow" refers to one whom the whole world refuses to help, leaving him like a single man.</margin>
<margin>6. This implies the world abandoned them of its own accord.</margin>

<summary>Xunzi defines true kingship not by hereditary right or the possession of records, but by the ability to maintain order through ritual and the support of the people. He argues that tyrants like Jie and Zhou did not simply lose their empires but were abandoned because they lacked virtue.</summary>
<keywords>Xunzi, Correct Discourse, Kingship, Tang of Shang, King Wu of Zhou, Jie of Xia, King Zhou of Shang, Virtue, Ritual and Righteousness</keywords>
